## A boardroom needs more than a table that fits

When buying office furniture in Newcastle, a meeting room can look like a straightforward order: one table and some chairs. In practice, the way people enter, sit, present, connect a laptop and join a video call can change which setting works.

Start with the meeting, then test the furniture and equipment together. This guide is a room-brief method, not a prescribed occupancy or clearance standard. Your designer, building advisers and relevant specialists should assess suitability for the actual premises and users.

**Use the working brief:** [Download the meeting-room planning worksheet (TXT)](/guides/meeting-room-furniture-brief-newcastle.txt). It contains a room schedule, three-option comparison and acceptance checks. Copy it into your project notes; no email is needed.

For the buying route, browse [YOF meeting-room furniture](https://www.yourofficefurniture.com.au/collections/meeting-rooms), or [request a coordinated furniture quote](/resources/furniture-quote#furniture-quote-form) for the whole setting.

## 1. Define the meetings before counting chairs

List the activities the room must support. A short internal discussion, a client presentation and a remote workshop can require different seating arrangements, table use and technology. Record usual attendance separately from the occasional maximum and identify anyone who needs a different setup.

| Meeting type | Questions for the brief |
| --- | --- |
| Internal discussion | How many people attend regularly, and what do they bring? |
| Client presentation | Where do visitors enter, sit and see the presentation? |
| Video meeting | Can remote participants see and hear the people taking part? |
| Training or workshop | Are laptops, shared materials or a different layout needed? |
| Multi-use room | Who resets the furniture, where are spare items stored, and how often does the layout change? |

Avoid turning the maximum headcount into the default order without testing the room. A smaller everyday setting with a separately assessed alternative may be more useful than a crowded permanent arrangement.

## 2. Measure the room and furniture in use

Record the internal room dimensions, door position and swing, windows, fixed cabinetry, columns and the proposed screen location. Check the actual chairs and table dimensions rather than relying on a photograph or the product's seat-count label.

Test the layout with chairs pulled out, people moving and cupboards in use. Ask your designer to check access and circulation for the actual workplace, including the needs of different users. A catalogue table described as seating a certain number does not certify that the room can accommodate that setting.

Mark unknown measurements on the brief. An approximate floor plan is useful for an initial conversation; it should not silently become a verified order drawing.

## 3. Choose the table base as well as the top

Compare table shape, top dimensions, finish, support structure and how the parts are delivered. Leg placement can affect where chairs fit. A central base, multiple legs and a modular arrangement create different opportunities and constraints.

Ask for a dimensioned product drawing where available. Check whether power modules, cable paths or equipment locations conflict with the base or the users' seating positions. Confirm which accessories are included and which need a separate order.

For larger pieces, establish whether the top is one piece, split or assembled on site. A table that fits in the room can still be difficult to get through the delivery route.

## 4. Compare chairs with the table and tasks

Record the chair width, arm height, adjustment options, base and movement on the actual floor surface. Check how the chairs fit around and under the selected table. Consider the length and type of meetings and the users' requirements when comparing options.

Where suitable samples or demonstrations are available, test the proposed setting before approval. Ask a competent ergonomic or WHS adviser about individual needs. A general label such as “ergonomic” is not evidence that one chair suits every person or task.

Comcare's workstation guidance considers equipment, tasks, adjustability and different users together. It is a useful principle for the brief, not a product endorsement or a prescribed boardroom layout. See our [Newcastle chair buying guide](/blog/office-chairs-newcastle) for product-comparison questions.

## 5. Bring the AV and electrical team into the furniture decision

Before approving a table, clarify the screen, camera, microphone, presentation equipment, charging and cable-management requirements with your IT or AV provider. Ask them to test the intended use and identify the furniture interfaces they need.

Record who supplies each item, who installs it and who tests it. Keep regulated electrical and other trade work with the appropriately appointed people. Furniture assembly does not automatically include electrical installation, network configuration or AV commissioning.

A useful acceptance test is an ordinary meeting: a visitor arrives, a laptop connects, people can see the material and remote participants can take part. Agree who confirms the result instead of treating a powered-on screen as the whole test.

## 6. Compare three complete settings

Use the same room brief for each proposal. Mark a missing answer as unconfirmed, not included or free.

| Compare each setting | Evidence or clarification |
| --- | --- |
| Table | Model, dimensions, base, finish and delivered components |
| Seating | Quantity, model, dimensions, adjustments and intended use |
| Equipment interfaces | Required openings, modules, brackets and cable paths |
| Scope boundaries | Furniture, electrical, data and AV responsibilities |
| Delivery | Building route, access bookings, assembly, placement and packaging |
| Timing and support | Availability for the exact finish, approvals, warranty terms and defect contact |

A complete installed scope can be more useful than the lowest table price. Our [installed furniture cost comparison](/blog/compare-office-furniture-quotes-installed-cost) includes a clearly hypothetical worked example, while the [Newcastle furniture budget guide](/blog/office-furniture-budget-newcastle) helps connect the room with the wider order.

## 7. Plan Newcastle building access before confirming delivery

For the actual building, ask about loading arrangements, lift capacity and dimensions, stairs, doorways, delivery windows and any required inductions. Do not assume every Newcastle CBD, Honeysuckle or suburban workplace has the same restrictions.

Give the supplier a marked plan identifying the room and product labels. Agree who receives the goods, checks damage, approves placement and records incomplete items. Confirm whether furniture packaging is removed and whether other work must finish before installation.

If the room remains in use, plan the interruption and temporary meeting arrangements. Keep those operational decisions separate from a supplier's estimated dispatch date. Use the [Newcastle furniture installation checklist](/blog/office-furniture-installation-checklist-newcastle) for the full sequence.

## The meeting-room order checklist

1. Record usual meetings, attendance, visitors and user requirements.
2. Verify the measured room and delivery route.
3. Test table and chairs in use, not just in their stored positions.
4. Check table supports, equipment interfaces and the exact finish.
5. Confirm IT, AV and trade responsibilities with the relevant providers.
6. Compare complete settings on the same installed scope.
7. Agree availability, access, placement and acceptance checks.
8. Keep product references, instructions, warranty terms and outstanding actions.

## Put the room brief to work

YOS supplies and coordinates commercial furniture for Newcastle, Lake Macquarie and Hunter workplaces, with projects supported Australia-wide. Frank Smith, Head of Furniture, guides furniture briefs, selection, schedules and delivery requirements as part of the YOS team. [Meet the team](/about).

Browse [meeting-room furniture](https://www.yourofficefurniture.com.au/collections/meeting-rooms) and [seating](https://www.yourofficefurniture.com.au/collections/seating), or [send your room brief for a quote](/resources/furniture-quote#furniture-quote-form). Samples, availability and installation arrangements are confirmed for the particular products and site.

For building or services changes beyond the furniture order, discuss the separate [client-side FitOut project-management service](/office-fitout). YOS does not act as the builder or head contractor.
